article_title: A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers
citation: Eugenio Tufino. (2026). A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers. https://huggingface.co/spaces
title: Five-agent DPT simulated classroom on a static-friction problem
description: A simulated class of five AI students, each embodying a distinct point of failure in the reasoning process: Davide (Hazards A+B), Elena (Hazard C), Tommaso (Hazard D), Chiara (in transition) and Andrea (a near-expert peer). It runs on an LLM via a Gradio application on Hugging Face Spaces, with personas defined entirely in the system prompt, session reset and one-click export of the anonymised conversation log. Named agents respond, with roughly 30% probability a second agent intervenes, and an open question draws two to four responses.
requirements: Requires a valid API key from a supported LLM provider, supplied by the user; no specialised infrastructure or model training is needed.
constraints: The hazards are reified into stable characters — a deliberate pedagogical simplification the framework itself warns against.
Participants noted the environment's limits as a proxy for real classrooms: "real students do not ask all those questions".
target_learners: prospective physics teachers in MSc programs
target_learning_goals: responding in real time to student reasoning with differentiated questioning strategies
examples: In one opening exchange, within three turns the participant elicited Davide's intuitive rule and set up a conflict with the observed situation.
key_sources: Eugenio Tufino. (2026). A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers. https://huggingface.co/spaces

article_title: A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers
citation: Eugenio Tufino. (2026). A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers. https://huggingface.co/spaces
title: Dual-process reasoning hazards framework with hazard-matched questioning strategies
description: Dual-process theories describe reasoning as the interplay of a fast, automatic Process 1 producing a provisional mental model and a slow, effortful Process 2 that evaluates it. Physics education research maps four hazards along the reasoning path: intuition may supply an incorrect first model (A); a confident reasoner may accept it without scrutiny (B); analysis may be biased towards rationalising the initial answer (C); or the mindware may be insufficient to detect the error (D). The course matched each hazard to a questioning strategy from the ISLE framework: guiding questions for A and B, conflict between formula and known result for C, and falling-back questions for D.
requirements: Each hazard was explicitly matched to a strategy in the lesson preceding the simulation.
constraints: Hazards are failure points of a process, not student types; reifying them as stable characters is a simplification.
target_learners: secondary-school physics students whose reasoning the teachers diagnose
target_learning_goals: selecting questions matched to the hazard
examples: Lesson 1 used the block-and-magnet sequence so participants encountered the framework as an explanation of their own reasoning: 93% answered the screening question correctly while the class split 50%–50% on the magnet question.
key_sources: Eugenio Tufino. (2026). A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers. https://huggingface.co/spaces

article_title: Verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments: A meta-analysis.
citation: Adesope, O. O., & Nesbit, J. C. (2012). Verbal Redundancy in Multimedia Learning Environments: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026147
title: Dual Processing Theory of Multimedia Learning as an account of verbal redundancy effects
description: The article reviews the dual processing theory of multimedia learning (DPTML), which rests on three assumptions: working memory has partially independent auditory and visual systems, each limited in capacity, and learning occurs when information in each mode is selected, organized, and integrated. DPTML predicts that learners concurrently reading and hearing a message hold verbal and visual representations in functionally distinct working memories, so "Information that is misperceived in one modality is available through the other modality." The article uses DPTML as the theoretical prediction that spoken–written presentations should exceed spoken-only and written-only ones, a prediction the meta-analysis partly disconfirms.
requirements: Concurrent presentation of verbal information in both spoken and written modes during multimedia learning
constraints: The meta-analysis found no advantage of spoken–written over written-only presentation, contradicting DPTML's prediction of greater learning from spoken–written than either unimodal format
target_learning_goals: retention and transfer of multimedia instructional content
examples: The meta-analysis tested DPTML's prediction across 57 independent effect sizes comparing spoken–written, spoken-only, and written-only presentations
key_sources: Adesope, O. O., & Nesbit, J. C. (2012). Verbal Redundancy in Multimedia Learning Environments: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026147

article_title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
citation: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6
title: The Deteriorating Patient (DP) role play as an interactive, contextualized extension of medical PBL addressing its text-based, decontextualized, cognition-only limitations
description: The DP role play is a medical simulation in which students collaboratively manage a deteriorating patient by playing on-call student, junior resident, and senior resident roles, while the teacher plays the duty nurse and the patient. It retains PBL's hypothesize-and-test structure but, per the article, "instead of reading about a case, the students are role-playing a case." It was created to address Hoffmann and Ritchie's three PBL limitations by providing "an interactive, contextualized environment, where both cognitive and affective considerations are met." Student questioning is guided by the ABCDEF emergency algorithm and by nurse feedback on vital signs and labs.
requirements: Students take differentiated roles (on-call student, junior and senior residents) with the teacher simulating the patient and duty nurse
Scenarios simulate emergencies students will encounter in hospital wards and emergency rooms
constraints: Originally only about half the students in a class could participate in each one-hour role play due to time limitations; this case study added small-group collaboration to include all students
target_learners: third-year medical students in internal medicine
target_learning_goals: emergency decision making under deteriorating conditions
managing anxiety and communication with patients
examples: Students ask the nurse about vital signs, breathing, and circulation; when a student runs into difficulty the teacher prompts calling the junior resident, then the senior resident, simulating how real emergencies unfold
key_sources: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6

article_title: Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology
citation: Slomowitz R. F., Narayan A. J., & McGrath L. M. (2025). Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102090
title: Developmental psychopathology resilience framework: resilience as a dynamic process of better-than-expected outcomes in the context of risk
description: The paper adapts the DP resilience framework to LD research, defining resilience as "the process of obtaining better-than-expected outcomes or developmentally appropriate functioning due to successful adaptation in the context of risk or adversity". Two core tenets are that risk is a prerequisite for resilience (without adversity the mechanisms are called competence) and that resilience is a dynamic process, not a trait or single-point outcome. The framework distinguishes promotive from protective factors as quantifiable resilience mechanisms.
requirements: Risk or adversity must be present as a prerequisite condition for resilience mechanisms to be identified
constraints: The paper focuses on individual-level factors because these are most commonly studied in academic resilience research, with less focus on systemic factors
target_learners: children at risk for learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: academic outcomes in reading and math despite risk for learning disabilities
key_sources: Slomowitz R. F., Narayan A. J., & McGrath L. M. (2025). Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102090

article_title: Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education
citation: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1
title: Three DPL implementation models: supplementary, substitute, and integrative
description: The article identifies three models for implementing Digital Personalised Learning: 'supplementary (DPL outside regular instruction such as additional technology-led sessions or afterschool programmes)', 'substitute (DPL replaces traditional teaching with all instruction delivered through technology)', and 'integrative (featuring both teacher and technology, integrating teacher, learner, and classroom interactions, with technology supporting teaching and learning)'. The study notes supplementary models are most common in LMICs, with UNICEF identifying 35 of 40 personalised learning tools used for supplemental learning, resulting in limited teacher involvement.
requirements: Implementation requires consideration of how DPL is aligned with teachers' daily classroom routines and curriculum content.
constraints: The article acknowledges Van Schoors et al.'s caution against oversimplifying classifications of DPL implementation.
target_learners: Early-years and primary learners in low- and middle-income countries
key_sources: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1

article_title: The use of deliberate practice in simulation-based surgical training for laparoscopic surgery - a systematic review.
citation: Wickramasinghe D, Vincent J. (2025). The use of deliberate practice in simulation-based surgical training for laparoscopic surgery – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07613-w
title: Structure simulation-based surgical training according to deliberate practice principles, including immediate feedback and stepwise task progression
description: The review concludes that DP is a useful instructional design tool for structuring SBST and that "Strict adherence to DP, however, is likely to produce superior training results than conventional training". Programs should incorporate immediate feedback, structured task progression, and repetition with attention to effort constraints between sessions.
requirements: Requires immediate feedback, stepwise task progression, and repeated practice sessions
constraints: Limited by resource requirements, particularly instructor commitment and equipment capable of real-time metrics
key_sources: Wickramasinghe D, Vincent J. (2025). The use of deliberate practice in simulation-based surgical training for laparoscopic surgery – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07613-w

article_title: Direct Problem-Based Learning (DPBL): A Framework for Integrating Direct Instruction and Problem-Based Learning Approach
citation: Sri Winarno, Kalaiarasi Sonai Muthu & Lew Sook Ling. (2017). Direct Problem-Based Learning (DPBL): A Framework for Integrating Direct Instruction and Problem-Based Learning Approach. International Education Studies, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p119
title: Direct Problem-Based Learning (DPBL) integrated model
description: DPBL is a conceptual framework combining direct instruction with problem-based learning activities, designed to improve students' knowledge, creative thinking, and teamwork skills. The article describes it as "a combination of the Direct Instruction and Problem-Based Learning activities" and structures it in three phases covering introduction and identification, application and solution, and evaluation and conclusion. It was modified from the UTM PBL model and applied to a third-year Computer Networks subject.
requirements: Lecturers take the role of presenting theory and objectives, presenting the problem, and monitoring group activities while students work in small groups
constraints: The article considers the approach appropriate for the high levels of education
examples: The model was implemented over one semester in two departments, with the DPBL group session lasting 2 hours per week for 3 weeks in groups of five to six students
key_sources: Sri Winarno, Kalaiarasi Sonai Muthu & Lew Sook Ling. (2017). Direct Problem-Based Learning (DPBL): A Framework for Integrating Direct Instruction and Problem-Based Learning Approach. International Education Studies, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p119

article_title: Direct Problem-Based Learning (DPBL): A Framework for Integrating Direct Instruction and Problem-Based Learning Approach
citation: Sri Winarno, Kalaiarasi Sonai Muthu & Lew Sook Ling. (2017). Direct Problem-Based Learning (DPBL): A Framework for Integrating Direct Instruction and Problem-Based Learning Approach. International Education Studies, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p119
title: Three-phase DPBL lesson sequence: introduction and identification, application and solution, evaluation and conclusion
description: The DPBL classroom pattern organises a lesson into three phases. In Phase 1 the lecturer introduces the lesson, divides students into small groups, presents theory and the problem, and monitors group discussion. In Phase 2 "The groups define the real world problem and final solution" and search and synthesise related data while the lecturer provides advice. In Phase 3 groups present their work reports and "The lecturer explains and summarises the concepts and then closes the lesson."
requirements: Small groups of five to six members with explained roles and work criteria
Lecturer monitoring of group activities and provision of advice and suggestions
examples: Figure 3 depicts the teaching and learning situation using DPBL activities in the Computer Networks subject
key_sources: Sri Winarno, Kalaiarasi Sonai Muthu & Lew Sook Ling. (2017). Direct Problem-Based Learning (DPBL): A Framework for Integrating Direct Instruction and Problem-Based Learning Approach. International Education Studies, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p119

article_title: Effects of Second Step Curriculum on Behavioral and Academic Outcomes in 5th and 8th Grade Students: A Longitudinal Study on Character Development
citation: Top, N., Liew, J., & Luo, W. (2016). Effects of Second Step curriculum on behavioral and academic outcomes in 5th and 8th grade students: A longitudinal study on character development. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 10(1), 24-47.
title: Discipline Point System (DPS) and Prosocial Behavior Rating System (PBRS): teacher observation-based behavioral measurement tools
description: The charter school system required all teachers to use the Discipline Point System (DPS) (α = .77) and the Prosocial Behavior Rating System (PBRS) (α = .65) "to observe and record data on students' problem and prosocial school behaviors". The DPS assigns negative points for specific problem behaviors (e.g., talking back to teacher, using profanity), while the PBRS assigns positive points for prosocial behaviors (e.g., helping a fellow student, volunteering). Teachers were trained, informed parents and students, and provided weekly behavior status updates.
requirements: Teacher training on the systems
Informing parents and students about the point systems
Weekly communication of behavior status to parents
constraints: The measurement system for prosocial school behaviors was not designed to record repeated occurrences of prosocial behaviors but only once a day
examples: DPS point values range from -1 (e.g., running in hallway) to -5 (e.g., using profanity); PBRS point values range from 1 (e.g., having all supplies) to 5 (e.g., served Saturday detention)
key_sources: Top, N., Liew, J., & Luo, W. (2016). Effects of Second Step curriculum on behavioral and academic outcomes in 5th and 8th grade students: A longitudinal study on character development. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 10(1), 24-47. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1167262

article_title: Students' Feedback of mDPBL Approach and the Learning Impact towards Computer Networks Teaching and Learning
citation: Winarno, S., Muthu, K. S., & Ling, L. S. (2018). Students’ feedback of mdpbl approach and the learning impact towards computer networks teaching and learning. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(1), 37-43. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.1.37
title: Direct Problem-Based Learning (DPBL) as a combination of direct instruction and problem-based learning
description: The article defines DPBL as a hybrid teaching approach: "The DPBL approach is a combination of DIA and PBL approach". It draws on direct instruction characteristics (face-to-face delivery, deliberate sequencing, small groups) and problem-based learning characteristics (student-centred, real-world ill-structured problems, teacher as facilitator, groups no larger than nine). In this study DPBL was paired with multimedia learning and implemented with groups of four to six members presenting work reports.
requirements: Small groups of four to six students
Teacher acting as facilitator rather than only delivering content
constraints: Applied here to a single abstract technical subject, Computer Networks
target_learners: University students in computer science-related departments
target_learning_goals: Problem-solving skills, creative thinking, teamwork, and subject knowledge
examples: Students were divided into small groups of four to six members, topics were presented using multimedia learning, and groups presented work reports.
key_sources: Winarno, S., Muthu, K. S., & Ling, L. S. (2018). Students’ feedback of mdpbl approach and the learning impact towards computer networks teaching and learning. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(1), 37-43. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.1.37

article_title: Interactive E-Learning Module: Enhancing Panoramic Radiograph Interpretation Skills of Dental Students.
citation: S. Y. Math, O. S. Sultan, M. F. B. Z. Anuar, and C. Pacheco‐Pereira, "Interactive E‐Learning Module: Enhancing Panoramic Radiograph Interpretation Skills of Dental Students." Journal of Dental Education 90, no. 1 (2026): 136–146. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.13923
title: Two interactive e-learning modules: DPR interpretation and a virtual dental clinic for communication skills
description: The article developed two e-learning modules using the ADDIE model, built in Articulate Storyline 360 and delivered via Moodle for self-directed, asynchronous use over four weeks. The first module trains DPR interpretation with "high‐resolution annotated images" and five patient-based cases (generalized periodontitis, periapical pathology, odontogenic cysts, dental trauma, fibro‐osseous lesions). The second is a case-based virtual dental clinic using role-play scripts and interactive patient simulations with a three-star patient satisfaction rating for immediate feedback on communication.
requirements: Access via a learning management system (Moodle) on personal devices; content aligned with the final-year dental curriculum
constraints: The VDC did not fully replicate real-world patient interactions, particularly non-verbal communication and empathetic engagement, per student feedback
target_learning_goals: DPR interpretation (anatomical landmarks, errors, pathology diagnosis)
examples: Students completed interactive quizzes, annotated high-resolution DPR images, and role-play conversations selecting structured responses to patient inquiries
key_sources: S. Y. Math, O. S. Sultan, M. F. B. Z. Anuar, and C. Pacheco‐Pereira, "Interactive E‐Learning Module: Enhancing Panoramic Radiograph Interpretation Skills of Dental Students." Journal of Dental Education 90, no. 1 (2026): 136–146. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.13923

article_title: The effect of self-reflection on the outcomes of online clinical skills training: a comparative study.
citation: Hoang April, Hepburn Stevie-Jae, Morawska Alina, Sanders Matthew R. (2025). The effect of self-reflection on the outcomes of online clinical skills training: a comparative study. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10425-8
title: Declarative–procedural–reflective (DPR) model of professional skill acquisition
description: The article adopts Bennett-Levy's DPR model, which "outlines three interconnected systems of knowledge processing that are crucial for developing expertise: declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, and reflective knowledge." Declarative knowledge covers facts and theory, procedural knowledge the application of skills in practice, and reflective knowledge the capacity to analyse experiences, integrate feedback, and refine skills. Effective training relies on integrating all three systems; reflection is often triggered by discrepancies between expected and actual outcomes. The study tests whether prompting the reflective system in an asynchronous module improves outcomes.
requirements: Training that develops professional competence should engage all three systems rather than declarative content alone
constraints: The model was applied to a brief, single-module training on conducting an initial intake interview, not to full training programs
target_learners: pre- and post-licensure health, allied health, and social science professionals
target_learning_goals: clinical consultation skills for intake interviews about child behaviour problems
examples: The study operationalized the reflective system as self-reflection prompts plus written reflection activities and a mindfulness exercise embedded in the training module
key_sources: Hoang April, Hepburn Stevie-Jae, Morawska Alina, Sanders Matthew R. (2025). The effect of self-reflection on the outcomes of online clinical skills training: a comparative study. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10425-8

article_title: Deliberate Practice Supervision to Enhance the Effectiveness of Behavioral Activation for Depression: A Case Study.
citation: Sacks, D. (2025). Deliberate Practice Supervision to Enhance the Effectiveness of Behavioral Activation for Depression: A Case Study. Journal of Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1002/jclp.23786
title: Five-step DP supervision session structure: observe, set goal, tailor practice, rehearse, assign homework
description: The article prints a five-step structure for a DP supervision session: "1. Find a skill deficit through direct observation of performance. 2. Translate the deficit into a learning goal based on supervisor feedback. 3. Design personally tailored practice to achieve the goal. 4. Perform behavioral rehearsal with ongoing feedback. 5. Plan homework." Each step is demonstrated with case vignettes, including video review to locate a deficit and rehearsal against a paused recording of a real session moment.
requirements: Video or direct observation of real therapy performance to identify skill deficits
Skill criteria stated clearly enough to guide rehearsal and feedback
constraints: Within time limitations of clinical settings, observing a challenging moment is often enough rather than a sample of videos
target_learners: therapists in supervision learning structured treatment protocols
target_learning_goals: translating observed performance deficits into rehearsed behavioral skills
examples: Session 1: supervisor and supervisee watched ~5 minutes of video, identified the fix-it urge as the deficit, set the goal of refraining from solutions, rehearsed against the paused recording, and assigned homework repeating the practice
key_sources: Sacks, D. (2025). Deliberate Practice Supervision to Enhance the Effectiveness of Behavioral Activation for Depression: A Case Study. Journal of Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1002/jclp.23786

article_title: Deliberate Practice Supervision to Enhance the Effectiveness of Behavioral Activation for Depression: A Case Study.
citation: Sacks, D. (2025). Deliberate Practice Supervision to Enhance the Effectiveness of Behavioral Activation for Depression: A Case Study. Journal of Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1002/jclp.23786
title: Choose clearly defined, behaviorally described treatments as the vehicle for DP skill training
description: The article recommends training skills within treatments whose interventions are described in simple behavioral terms, because "The more clearly defined a skill is, the easier it will be to practice it, and no less importantly, to evaluate the resulting improvement in both therapist skill level and client wellbeing." Behavioral Activation was chosen for this reason, and because its motivation-facilitation nuances are not overtly stated in protocols and thus benefit most from direct observation and rehearsal.
requirements: A treatment protocol with clearly defined, behaviorally describable interventions
constraints: BA only helps some clients, not all; the article frames this case as improving the therapist rather than the therapy
target_learners: CBT therapists and supervisors selecting training cases
target_learning_goals: rehearsable therapy micro-skills within a structured protocol
examples: The BA intervention for rumination was decomposed into three sub-skills: validate client perspective, make the client aware of rumination and its costs, and suggest alternative behaviors
key_sources: Sacks, D. (2025). Deliberate Practice Supervision to Enhance the Effectiveness of Behavioral Activation for Depression: A Case Study. Journal of Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1002/jclp.23786

article_title: Advances in clinical pharmacy education in Germany: a quasi-experimental single-blinded study to evaluate a patient-centred clinical pharmacy course in psychiatry.
citation: Dircks Monika, Mayr Andreas, Freidank Annette, Kornhuber Johannes, Dörje Frank, Friedland Kristina. (2017). Advances in clinical pharmacy education in Germany: a quasi-experimental single-blinded study to evaluate a patient-centred clinical pharmacy course in psychiatry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1092-z
title: DPhG Clinical Pharmacy working group's 10 statements on effective clinical pharmacy teaching
description: In 2004, the "Clinical Pharmacy" working group of the German Pharmaceutical Society (DPhG) published 10 statements on the most effective use of teaching time in clinical pharmacy education. The article reports that these statements include: patient notes and data should play a central role; direct patient contact is desirable; clinical working pharmacists and physicians should be involved in teaching; and to ensure case-based and interactive learning, small learning groups should be formed. The stated aim is to enable students to support patients and medical staff in order to ensure the best possible medication use, taking into account patients' medical history and current medication use. The ward-based course evaluated in this article was designed to align with these statements.
requirements: Patient notes and data playing a central role in teaching
Direct patient contact
Involvement of clinical working pharmacists and physicians in teaching
Small learning groups for case-based and interactive learning
target_learning_goals: supporting patients and medical staff to ensure the best possible medication use
examples: The DPhG statements guided the design of the ward-based course evaluated in this study, which incorporated direct patient contact, small groups, and involvement of a clinical working pharmacist as teacher practitioner
key_sources: Dircks Monika, Mayr Andreas, Freidank Annette, Kornhuber Johannes, Dörje Frank, Friedland Kristina. (2017). Advances in clinical pharmacy education in Germany: a quasi-experimental single-blinded study to evaluate a patient-centred clinical pharmacy course in psychiatry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1092-z

article_title: Validation of the 5-item doctor-patient communication competency instrument for medical students (DPCC-MS) using two years of assessment data.
citation: Renaud Jean-Sébastien; Côté Luc. (2017). Validation of the 5-item doctor-patient communication competency instrument for medical students (DPCC-MS) using two years of assessment data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1026-9
title: DPCC-MS: a 5-item end-of-rotation doctor-patient communication assessment instrument for medical students
description: The DPCC-MS is a short summative assessment instrument developed at Laval University, based on the Patient Centered Clinical Method framework, providing "a global summative end-of-rotation assessment of doctor-patient communication". Each of its five items is rated on a four-point performance scale (Superior = 4, Expected = 3, Borderline = 2, Insufficient = 1), with a Not applicable option coded as missing, and item scores are averaged into a single synthetic score.
requirements: Used at the end of clinical rotations as part of a standardized summative evaluation form alongside other competency assessments
constraints: Excludes two PCCM components not specific to doctor-patient communication, namely incorporating prevention and health promotion and being realistic
examples: Administered at the end of each three-to-six-week clinical rotation at Laval University between 2011 and 2013
key_sources: Renaud Jean-Sébastien; Côté Luc. (2017). Validation of the 5-item doctor-patient communication competency instrument for medical students (DPCC-MS) using two years of assessment data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1026-9
